claim: Cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of death worldwide due to the inability of adult heart to regenerate after injury.
source: Cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of death worldwide due to the inability of adult heart to regenerate after injury.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Narula et al., 1996; Bergmann et al., 2009; Bui et al., 2011) as indicated in the text.

claim: N6-methyladenosine (m6A) methylation is catalyzed by the enzyme methyltransferase-like 3 (Mettl3).
source: N6-methyladenosine (m6A) methylation catalyzed by the enzyme methyltransferase-like 3 (Mettl3) plays an important role in various physiological and pathological bioprocesses.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about m6A methylation and Mettl3's role as the catalytic enzyme.

claim: Knockdown of Mettl3 significantly increased the proliferation of cardiomyocytes and accelerated heart regeneration following heart injury in neonatal and adult mice.
source: Knockdown of Mettl3 significantly increased the proliferation of cardiomyocytes and accelerated heart regeneration following heart injury in neonatal and adult mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, as evidenced by multiple figures showing increased cardiomyocyte proliferation and improved heart regeneration outcomes.

claim: Mettl3 overexpression decreased cardiomyocyte proliferation and suppressed heart regeneration in postnatal mice.
source: However, Mettl3 overexpression decreased cardiomyocyte proliferation and suppressed heart regeneration in postnatal mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing the opposite effect of Mettl3 overexpression compared to knockdown.

claim: Fgf16 was identified as a downstream target of Mettl3-mediated m6A modification during postnatal heart regeneration.
source: Conjoint analysis of methylated RNA immunoprecipitation sequencing (MeRIP-seq) and RNA-seq identified Fgf16 as a downstream target of Mettl3-mediated m6A modification during postnatal heart regeneration.
evidence: This claim is supported by MeRIP-seq and RNA-seq data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Mettl3 negatively regulates Fgf16 mRNA expression in an m6A-Ythdf2-dependent manner.
source: RIP-qPCR and luciferase reporter assays revealed that Mettl3 negatively regulates Fgf16 mRNA expression in an m6A-Ythdf2-dependent manner.
evidence: This claim is supported by RIP-qPCR and luciferase reporter assay data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Silencing of Fgf16 suppressed the proliferation of cardiomyocytes.
source: The silencing of Fgf16 suppressed the proliferation of cardiomyocytes.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing reduced cardiomyocyte proliferation upon Fgf16 knockdown.

claim: Overexpression of ΔFgf16 (mutant Fgf16 with mutated m6A consensus sequence) significantly increased cardiomyocyte proliferation and accelerated heart regeneration in postnatal mice compared with wild-type Fgf16.
source: However, the overexpression of ΔFgf16, in which the m6A consensus sequence was mutated, significantly increased cardiomyocyte proliferation and accelerated heart regeneration in postnatal mice compared with wild-type Fgf16.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing the effects of wild-type and mutant Fgf16 overexpression.

claim: Complete cardiac regeneration occurs in neonatal mouse heart after ventricular resection at postnatal day 1 (p1), but this capacity is lost at p7.
source: It has been demonstrated that complete cardiac regeneration occurs in neonatal mouse heart after ventricular resection at postnatal day 1 (p1), but this capacity is lost at p7 (Porrello et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature (Porrello et al., 2011).

claim: Cardiac regeneration in neonatal mice is primarily mediated by cardiomyocyte proliferation.
source: It has been believed that cardiac regeneration in neonatal mice is primarily mediated by cardiomyocyte proliferation (Porrello et al., 2011; Mahmoud et al., 2013; Porrello et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Porrello et al., 2011; Mahmoud et al., 2013; Porrello et al., 2013).

claim: mRNA abundance does not correlate with protein expression in failing hearts.
source: Previous studies have reported that mRNA abundance does not correlate with protein expression in failing hearts (Brundel et al., 2001; Su et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Brundel et al., 2001; Su et al., 2015).

claim: Nuclear and cytosolic mRNA levels are not correlated in cardiomyocytes.
source: Moreover, nuclear and cytosolic mRNA levels are not correlated in cardiomyocytes (Preissl et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature (Preissl et al., 2015).

claim: More than 150 distinct chemical marks have been identified on cellular RNA.
source: Although more than 150 distinct chemical marks have been identified on cellular RNA (Boccaletto et al., 2018), the N6-methyladenosine (m6A) methylation catalyzed by the enzyme methyltransferase-like 3 (Mettl3) has been the most prevalent and best-characterized mRNA modification (Dominissini et al., 2012; Meyer et al., 2012; Fu et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature (Boccaletto et al., 2018).

claim: m6A methylation is the most prevalent and best-characterized mRNA modification.
source: Although more than 150 distinct chemical marks have been identified on cellular RNA (Boccaletto et al., 2018), the N6-methyladenosine (m6A) methylation catalyzed by the enzyme methyltransferase-like 3 (Mettl3) has been the most prevalent and best-characterized mRNA modification (Dominissini et al., 2012; Meyer et al., 2012; Fu et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Dominissini et al., 2012; Meyer et al., 2012; Fu et al., 2014).

claim: m6A plays an important role in gene regulation.
source: Recent studies have demonstrated that m6A plays an important role in gene regulation (Roundtree et al., 2017), animal development (Zhao et al., 2017; Frye et al., 2018), and human disease (Hsu et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2018; Paris et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature (Roundtree et al., 2017).

claim: m6A plays an important role in animal development.
source: Recent studies have demonstrated that m6A plays an important role in gene regulation (Roundtree et al., 2017), animal development (Zhao et al., 2017; Frye et al., 2018), and human disease (Hsu et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2018; Paris et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Zhao et al., 2017; Frye et al., 2018).

claim: m6A plays an important role in human disease.
source: Recent studies have demonstrated that m6A plays an important role in gene regulation (Roundtree et al., 2017), animal development (Zhao et al., 2017; Frye et al., 2018), and human disease (Hsu et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2018; Paris et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Hsu et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2018; Paris et al., 2019).

claim: Effectors of m6A pathways consist of 'writers', 'erasers', and 'readers' that respectively install, remove, and recognize methylation.
source: A number of studies have demonstrated that effectors of m6A pathways consist of 'writers', 'erasers', and 'readers' that respectively install, remove, and recognize methylation (Shi et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature (Shi et al., 2019).

claim: Mettl3 expression significantly increased from postnatal day 3 (p3) to p14 in neonatal mouse hearts.
source: Among these four genes, Mettl3 expression significantly increased from postnatal day 3 (p3) to p14 (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data presented in Figure 1A.

claim: Increased expression of Mettl3 in postnatal heart at p14 was detected at protein levels.
source: In agreement with qPCR result, increased expression of Mettl3 in postnatal heart at p14 was also detected in protein levels (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data presented in Figure 1B and C.

claim: Increased levels of m6A modification were detected at p14 compared with p3 and p7 in neonatal mouse hearts.
source: Increased levels of m6A modification were detected at p14 compared with p3 and p7 (Figure 1D), suggesting the lower levels of m6A modification within postnatal 7 days (the regenerative window).
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA-based m6A quantification data presented in Figure 1D.

claim: Apex resection injury increased the level of m6A modification by 65% at 5 dpr compared with sham hearts.
source: As shown in Figure 1F, apex resection injury increased the level of m6A modification by 65% at 5 dpr compared with sham hearts.
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA-based m6A quantification data presented in Figure 1F.

claim: The expression of Mettl3 was approximately increased up to 2-fold at 5 dpr compared with sham hearts.
source: Moreover, the expression of Mettl3 was approximately increased up to 2-fold at 5 dpr compared with sham hearts (Figure 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data presented in Figure 1G.

claim: The expression of Mettl3 rather than Mettl14 was greatly increased at 5 dpr compared with sham hearts.
source: Western blotting revealed that the expression of Mettl3 rather than Mettl14 was greatly increased at 5 dpr compared with sham hearts (Figure 1H–J).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data presented in Figure 1H-J.

claim: Mettl3 expression and m6A levels were increased in remote areas at 5 dpr compared with control groups.
source: In consistent with apical areas, our data showed that Mettl3 expression and m6A levels were also increased in remote areas at 5 dpr compared with control groups (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot and ELISA data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The m6A level in cardiomyocytes (CMs) is higher than that in non-cardiomyocytes (nCMs).
source: Our data showed that the m6A level in CMs is higher than that in nCMs, indicating the functional importance of m6A modification in CMs (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA-based m6A quantification data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Mettl3 expression was significantly increased in CMs rather than nCMs upon injury.
source: Our data showed that Mettl3 expression was significantly increased in CMs rather than nCMs upon injury (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Mettl3 knockdown significantly increased the percentage of EdU+ cells in H9c2 cardiomyocyte cell line.
source: The percentage of EdU+ cells was significantly increased by Mettl3 knockdown (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, C), suggesting elevated levels of proliferation in Mettl3-silencing cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by EdU incorporation assay data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, C.

claim: Cell number was greatly promoted by Mettl3 knockdown in H9c2 cells.
source: Indeed, cell number was also greatly promoted by siMettl3 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell counting data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Increased m6A levels were observed in Mettl3-overexpressing H9c2 cells compared with controls.
source: As expected, increased m6A levels were observed in the Mettl3-overexpressing cells compared with controls (Figure 2—figure supplement 1I, J).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence staining data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 1I, J.

claim: Both cell proliferation and count were remarkably suppressed by Mettl3 overexpression in H9c2 cells.
source: In contrast with the knockdown cells, both cell proliferation and count were remarkably suppressed by Mettl3 overexpression in H9c2 cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1K-M).
evidence: This claim is supported by EdU incorporation and cell counting data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 1K-M.

claim: Mettl3 knockdown leads to an increase in the percentage of Ki67+ cTnT+ cells in primary cardiomyocytes.
source: Ki67 and cTnT double staining revealed that Mettl3 knockdown (Figure 2A and B) leads to an increase in the percentage of Ki67+ cTnT+ cells, indicating an elevated proliferation level of primary cardiomyocytes (Figure 2E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence staining data presented in Figure 2E and F.

claim: Mettl3 overexpression suppressed the proliferation of primary cardiomyocytes as demonstrated by Ki67 and cTnT double staining.
source: In contrast, Mettl3 overexpression (Figure 2C and D) suppressed the proliferation of primary cardiomyocytes as demonstrated by Ki67 and cTnT double staining (Figure 2G and H).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence staining data presented in Figure 2G and H.

claim: The percentage of EdU+ cTnT+ cells was greatly increased by Mettl3 knockdown in primary cardiomyocytes.
source: In agreement with these results, EdU incorporation assay revealed that the percentage of EdU+ cTnT+ cells was greatly increased by Mettl3 knockdown (Figure 2I and J), indicating an elevated proliferation level of primary cardiomyocytes.
evidence: This claim is supported by EdU incorporation assay data presented in Figure 2I and J.

claim: The proliferation of primary cardiomyocytes was approximately suppressed by 48% by Mettl3 overexpression as demonstrated by nuclear EdU incorporation.
source: However, the proliferation of primary cardiomyocytes was approximately suppressed by 48% by Mettl3 overexpression as demonstrated by nuclear EdU incorporation (Figure 2K and L).
evidence: This claim is supported by EdU incorporation assay data presented in Figure 2K and L.

claim: AAV9-shRNA system induces modest expression of reporter gene in neonatal heart at 2 days post-injection (dpi), followed by substantial expression from 6 to 27 dpi.
source: Our results revealed that AAV9-shRNA system induces modest expression of reporter gene in neonatal heart at 2 days post-injection (dpi), followed by substantial expression from 6 to 27 dpi (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence staining data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Successful knockdown of Mettl3 in heart tissue at 0 dpr was confirmed by qPCR validation of Mettl3 mRNA expression.
source: Successful knockdown of Mettl3 in heart tissue at 0 dpr was confirmed by the qPCR validation of Mettl3 mRNA expression (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data presented in Figure 3B.

claim: Decreased expression of Mettl3 protein was demonstrated in primary cardiomyocytes isolated from ventricles at 0 dpr.
source: The decreased expression of Mettl3 protein (Figure 3C and D) and reduced m6A modification (Figure 3E) was further demonstrated in primary cardiomyocytes.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data presented in Figure 3C and D.

claim: Reduced m6A modification was demonstrated in primary cardiomyocytes isolated from ventricles at 0 dpr.
source: The decreased expression of Mettl3 protein (Figure 3C and D) and reduced m6A modification (Figure 3E) was further demonstrated in primary cardiomyocytes.
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA-based m6A quantification data presented in Figure 3E.

claim: Smaller cardiomyocyte size with no change in heart to body weight ratio was observed in Mettl3-silencing hearts compared with controls at 5 dpr.
source: Smaller cardiomyocyte size with no change in heart to body weight ratio was observed in Mettl3-silencing hearts compared with controls (Figure 3F–H), implying increased numbers of cardiomyocytes in Mettl3-deficient hearts.
evidence: This claim is supported by WGA staining and heart weight/body weight ratio data presented in Figure 3F-H.

claim: The percentage of pH3+ cTnT+ cells was significantly elevated by Mettl3 silencing both in apical and remote zones at 5 dpr.
source: Consistently, the percentage of pH3+ cTnT+ cells was significantly elevated by Mettl3 silencing both in apical (Figure 3I and J) and remote (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A, B) zones, indicating that Mettl3 knockdown really promotes the complete proliferation of cardiomyocytes in vivo.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence staining data presented in Figure 3I, J and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A, B.

claim: Increased percentage of AurkB+ cardiomyocytes was detected in cardiac apex in the Mettl3-deficient neonatal mice at 5 dpr.
source: Importantly, increased percentage of AurkB+ cardiomyocytes was also detected in cardiac apex in the Mettl3-deficient neonatal mice (Figure 3K–M), implying the increased cytokinesis of cardiomyocytes.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence staining data presented in Figure 3K-M.

claim: In vivo staining of Ki67 revealed that cardiomyocyte proliferation in the injured neonatal hearts was greatly increased by Mettl3 silencing in the apical and remote zones compared with controls at 5 dpr.
source: In agreement with above observation, in vivo staining of Ki67 further revealed that cardiomyocyte proliferation in the injured neonatal hearts was greatly increased by Mettl3 silencing in the apical (Figure 3N and O) and remote (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C, D) zones compared with controls.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence staining data presented in Figure 3N, O and Figure 3—figure supplement 2C, D.

claim: Nuclear EdU incorporation revealed that in vivo silencing of Mettl3 increased the percentage of EdU+ cTnT+ cells both in apical and remote cardiac tissues at 5 dpr.
source: Moreover, nuclear EdU incorporation revealed that in vivo silencing of Mettl3 increased the percentage of EdU+ cTnT+ cells both in apical (Figure 3P and Q) and remote (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E, F) cardiac tissues.
evidence: This claim is supported by EdU incorporation assay data presented in Figure 3P, Q and Figure 3—figure supplement 2E, F.

claim: Mettl3 knockdown has no significant effects on heart weight/body weight (HW/BW) ratio in homeostatic neonatal hearts without injury.
source: Our data showed that Mettl3 knockdown has no significant effects on heart weight/body weight (HW/BW) ratio compared with controls (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by heart weight/body weight ratio data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Cardiomyocyte size is comparable between Mettl3-silencing and control hearts in homeostatic neonatal hearts without injury.
source: WGA staining revealed that cardiomyocyte size is comparable between Mettl3-silencing and control hearts (Figure 3—figure supplement 3C, D).
evidence: This claim is supported by WGA staining data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 3C, D.

claim: No significant differences in cardiomyocyte proliferation were observed in Mettl3-silencing hearts compared with controls in homeostatic neonatal hearts without injury, as determined by EdU, Ki67, and pH3 staining.
source: Moreover, no significant differences in cardiomyocyte proliferation were observed in Mettl3-silencing hearts compared with controls, which were determined by EdU, Ki67, and pH3 staining (Figure 3—figure supplement 3E, J).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence staining data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 3E-J.

claim: Scar size in the cardiac apex at 14 dpr was decreased by 73% in Mettl3-deficient hearts compared with controls.
source: Histological analysis revealed that scar size in the cardiac apex at 14 dpr was decreased by 73% in Mettl3-deficient hearts compared with controls (Figure 4B and C), implying the accelerated heart regeneration.
evidence: This claim is supported by Masson's trichrome staining data presented in Figure 4B and C.

claim: Smaller scar sizes in Mettl3-deficient hearts were confirmed by whole heart images at 14 dpr.
source: In agreement with these results, smaller scar sizes in Mettl3-deficient hearts were also confirmed by whole heart images (Figure 4D–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by whole heart imaging data presented in Figure 4D-F.

claim: Cardiomyocyte size was much smaller in Mettl3-deficient hearts compared with controls at 14 dpr.
source: In addition, cardiomyocyte size was much smaller in Mettl3-deficient hearts compared with controls (Figure 4G and H).
evidence: This claim is supported by WGA staining data presented in Figure 4G and H.

claim: Increased left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) and fractional shortening (LVFS) were detected in Mettl3-deficient mice at 14 dpr.
source: As expected, increased left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) and fractional shortening (LVFS) were detected in Mettl3-deficient mice (Figure 4I–K), indicating that left ventricular systolic function was promoted by Mettl3 knockdown.
evidence: This claim is supported by echocardiography data presented in Figure 4I-K.

claim: The percentage of EdU+ cTnT+ cells both in apical and remote zones were significantly increased in Mettl3-deficient hearts compared with controls at 14 dpr.
source: Our data revealed that the percentage of EdU+ cTnT+ cells both in apical and remote zones were significantly increased in Mettl3-deficient hearts compared with controls (Figure 4L–O), implying that there are more proliferating cardiomyocytes during the whole period of 14 dpr.
evidence: This claim is supported by EdU incorporation assay data presented in Figure 4L-O.

claim: Mettl3 knockdown did not lead to significant changes in cardiomyocyte size, proliferation, as well as cardiac function in the homeostatic neonatal mice without injury.
source: In contract, Mettl3 knockdown did not lead to significant changes in cardiomyocyte size, proliferation, as well as cardiac function in the homeostatic neonatal mice without injury (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Cardiomyocyte proliferation in the injured neonatal hearts was significantly increased by Mettl3 knockdown at 3 dpr following apex resection at p7.
source: Ki67 staining revealed that cardiomyocyte proliferation in the apical zones of injured neonatal hearts was significantly increased by Mettl3 knockdown (Figure 4—figure supplement 2E-G).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence staining data presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 2E-G.

claim: Mettl3-silencing increased the percentage of pH3+ cTnT+ cells in apical myocardium at 3 dpr following apex resection at p7.
source: In addition, Mettl3-silencing increased the percentage of pH3+ cTnT+ cells in apical myocardium (Figure 4—figure supplement 2H-J).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence staining data presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 2H-J.

claim: Scar size in the cardiac apex was decreased in Mettl3-deficient hearts compared with controls at 21 dpr following apex resection at p7.
source: These results are agreement with the histological analysis at 21 dpr which revealed that scar size in the cardiac apex was decreased in Mettl3-deficient hearts compared with controls (Figure 4—figure supplement 2K), implying the improved heart regeneration.
evidence: This claim is supported by whole heart imaging data presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 2K.

claim: Improving cardiac function was detected in Mettl3-deficient heart at 21 dpr as demonstrated by the increased LVEF and LVFS values following apex resection at p7.
source: Moreover, improving cardiac function was detected in Mettl3-deficient heart at 21 dpr as demonstrated by the increased LVEF and LVFS values (Figure 4—figure supplement 2L-N).
evidence: This claim is supported by echocardiography data presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 2L-N.

claim: Overexpression of Mettl3 protein and increase in m6A modification at p3 was confirmed by western blotting and ELISA-based m6A quantification assay.
source: Overexpression of Mettl3 protein and increase in m6A modification at p3 was confirmed by western blotting (Figure 5B and C) and ELISA-based m6A quantification assay (Figure 5D), respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot and ELISA data presented in Figure 5B-D.

claim: Persistent overexpression of Mettl3 at 28 dpr was evidenced by qPCR and immunofluorescent staining.
source: Persistent overexpression of Mettl3 at 28 dpr was further evidenced by qPCR and immunofluorescent staining (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, B), this was further supported by the substantial expression of EGFP reporter gene (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR and immunofluorescence staining data presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-C.

claim: Trichrome staining results revealed an increase in fibrotic scar size in Mettl3-overexpressing hearts compared with controls at 28 dpr.
source: Trichrome staining results revealed an increase in fibrotic scar size in Mettl3-overexpressing hearts compared with controls (Figure 5E–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by Masson's trichrome staining data presented in Figure 5E-G.

claim: The larger scar size induced by Mettl3 overexpression was further confirmed by whole heart images in parallel with the increased HW/BW ratio at 28 dpr.
source: The larger scar size induced by Mettl3 overexpression was further confirmed by whole heart images in parallel with the increased HW/BW ratio (Figure 5H–J).
evidence: This claim is supported by whole heart imaging and heart weight/body weight ratio data presented in Figure 5H-J.

claim: Cardiomyocyte size was increased in response to Mettl3 overexpression at 28 dpr.
source: In agreement with these results, cardiomyocyte size was increased in response to Mettl3 overexpression at 28 dpr (Figure 5K and L).
evidence: This claim is supported by WGA staining data presented in Figure 5K and L.

claim: Mettl3 overexpression leads to decreases in LVEF and LVFS levels at 28 dpr.
source: Our data showed that Mettl3 overexpression leads to decreases in LVEF and LVFS levels (Figure 5M–O), indicating that left ventricular systolic function is attenuated by Mettl3 overexpression.
evidence: This claim is supported by echocardiography data presented in Figure 5M-O.

claim: No Ki67+ cardiomyocytes were detected in both control and Mettl3-overexpressing groups at 28 dpr.
source: Using the immunofluorescence staining with antibodies against Ki67 and pH3, no positive cardiomyocytes were detected in both groups at 28 dpr (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence staining data presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Cardiomyocyte proliferation in the apical and remote zones was remarkably suppressed by Mettl3 overexpression during the whole period of 28 days post-resection, as revealed by pulse-chase injection of EdU.
source: However, pulse-chase injection of EdU (Figure 5P) revealed that cardiomyocyte proliferation in the apical (Figure 5Q and S) and remote (Figure 5R and T) zones was remarkably suppressed by Mettl3 overexpression during the whole period of 28 days post-resection.
evidence: This claim is supported by EdU incorporation assay data presented in Figure 5P-T.

claim: Mettl3 overexpression did not change the HW/BW ratio and cardiomyocyte size in the postnatal mice without injury.
source: However, Mettl3 overexpression did not change the HW/BW ratio and cardiomyocyte size in the postnatal mice without injury (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A-D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 3A-D.

claim: Cardiomyocyte proliferation was not influenced by Mettl3 overexpression in the uninjured hearts.
source: EdU-pulse injection experiments showed that cardiomyocyte proliferation was not influenced by Mettl3 overexpression in the uninjured hearts (Figure 5—figure supplement 3E, F).
evidence: This claim is supported by EdU incorporation assay data presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 3E, F.

claim: There were no significant changes in cardiac function in the uninjured hearts upon Mettl3 overexpression.
source: In line with these results, there were no significant changes in cardiac function in the uninjured hearts upon Mettl3 overexpression (Figure 5—figure supplement 3G, H).
evidence: This claim is supported by echocardiography data presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 3G, H.

claim: Heart injury did not significantly increase Mettl3 expression in postnatal and adult mice at 5 days post-MI.
source: In contrast with neonatal mice model, heart injury did not significantly increase Mettl3 expression in postnatal and adult mice (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data presented in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Mettl3 deficiency significantly reduced the size of cardiomyocytes in the infarcted neonatal hearts at 5 dpM.
source: WGA staining results revealed that Mettl3 deficiency significantly reduced the size of cardiomyocytes in the infarcted neonatal hearts at 5 dpM (Figure 6B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by WGA staining data presented in Figure 6B and C.

claim: Mettl3 knockdown promotes the proliferation of cardiomyocytes in the border zone of infarcted neonatal hearts as evidenced by the increased percentage of Ki67+ cTnT+ cells at 5 dpM.
source: Ki67 and cTnT double staining revealed that Mettl3 knockdown promotes the proliferation of cardiomyocytes in the border zone of infarcted neonatal hearts as evidenced by the increased percentage of Ki67+ cTnT+ cells (Figure 6D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence staining data presented in Figure 6D and E.

claim: Increased percentage of pH3+ cTnT+ cells was detected in the border zone in the Mettl3-deficient hearts at 5 dpM.
source: Moreover, increased percentage of pH3+ cTnT+ cells was detected in the border zone in the Mettl3-deficient hearts at 5 dpM (Figure 6F and G).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence staining data presented in Figure 6F and G.

claim: Both HW/BW ratio and scar size were lower in the Mettl3-deficient heart compared with controls at 21 dpM.
source: We further analyzed the cardiac histology at 21 dpM and found that both HW/BW ratio and scar size were lower in the Mettl3-deficient heart compared with controls (Figure 6H–J).
evidence: This claim is supported by heart weight/body weight ratio and Masson's trichrome staining data presented in Figure 6H-J.

claim: Smaller size of cardiomyocytes was detected in the Mettl3-deficient hearts compared with controls at 21 dpM.
source: In agreement with these findings, smaller size of cardiomyocytes was also detected in the Mettl3-deficient hearts compared with controls (Figure 6K and L).
evidence: This claim is supported by WGA staining data presented in Figure 6K and L.

claim: Mettl3 deficiency significantly increases LVEF and LVFS levels compared with control hearts at 21 dpM.
source: Echocardiography analysis at 21 dpM showed that Mettl3 deficiency significantly increases LVEF and LVFS levels compared with control hearts (Figure 6M–O).
evidence: This claim is supported by echocardiography data presented in Figure 6M-O.

claim: HW/BW ratio and scar size were decreased by Mettl3 deficiency compared with controls at 14 dpM in adult mice.
source: At 14 dpM, HW/BW ratio and scar size were decreased by Mettl3 deficiency compared with controls (Figure 7C–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by heart weight/body weight ratio and Masson's trichrome staining data presented in Figure 7C-E.

claim: The decreased HW/BW ratio and scar size were also observed in the Mettl3-deficient hearts compared with controls at 28 dpM in adult mice.
source: In line with these results, the decreased HW/BW ratio and scar size were also observed in the Mettl3-deficient hearts compared with controls at 28 dpM (Figure 7F–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by heart weight/body weight ratio and Masson's trichrome staining data presented in Figure 7F-H.

claim: Mettl3 deficiency leads to a little increase in LVEF and LVFS levels at 0 dpM (prior to MI) in adult mice.
source: Our data showed that Mettl3 deficiency leads to a little increase in LVEF and LVFS levels at 0 dpM (prior to MI).
evidence: This claim is supported by echocardiography data presented in Figure 7I-K.

claim: Increased levels of LVEF and LVFS were detected in Mettl3-deficient hearts at 28 dpM compared with control hearts in adult mice.
source: However, increased levels of LVEF and LVFS were detected in Mettl3-deficient hearts at 28 dpM compared with control hearts, respectively (Figure 7I–K).
evidence: This claim is supported by echocardiography data presented in Figure 7I-K.

claim: Mettl3 deficiency greatly increased the proliferation of cardiomyocytes in the border zone of infarction in adult mice at 14 dpM, as indicated by the increased percentage of Ki67+ cTnT+ cells.
source: Ki67 staining results showed that Mettl3 deficiency greatly increased the proliferation of cardiomyocytes in the border zone of infarction, as indicated by the increased percentage of Ki67+ cTnT+ cells (Figure 7L and M).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence staining data presented in Figure 7L and M.

claim: Increased percentage of Ki67+ cTnT+ cells was detected in the Mettl3-deficient hearts in the remote zone in comparison with control hearts in adult mice at 14 dpM.
source: In consistent with border zone, increased percentage of Ki67+ cTnT+ cells was also detected in the Mettl3-deficient hearts in the remote zone in comparison with control hearts (Figure 7N and O).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence staining data presented in Figure 7N and O.

claim: The GGACU motif is highly enriched in m6A sites in both sham and apex-resected hearts.
source: MeRIP-seq revealed that the GGACU motif is highly enriched in m6A sites in both sham and apex-resected hearts (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by MeRIP-seq data presented in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A.

claim: m6A peaks are particularly abundant in the vicinity of stop codons.
source: Moreover, m6A peaks are particularly abundant in the vicinity of stop codons (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by MeRIP-seq data presented in Figure 8—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The m6A peak distribution decreased in 5' untranslated region (5'UTR) in apex-resected hearts, whereas there was an increase in coding regions (CDS) and stop codon regions compared with sham operated hearts.
source: However, the m6A peak distribution decreased in 5' untranslated region (5'UTR) in apex-resected hearts, whereas there was an increase in coding regions (CDS) and stop codon regions compared with sham operated hearts (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by MeRIP-seq data presented in Figure 8—figure supplement 1B.

claim: An increase in total m6A peaks and m6A-tagged mRNAs was detected in injured hearts.
source: As expected, an increase in total m6A peaks and m6A-tagged mRNAs was detected in injured hearts (Figure 8—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by MeRIP-seq data presented in Figure 8—figure supplement 1D.

claim: A total of 750 genes (635 upregulated and 115 downregulated) were identified with a 2-fold m6A change in a comparison of the sham-operated and apex-resected hearts.
source: In a comparison of the sham-operated and apex-resected hearts, a total of 750 genes (635 upregulated and 115 downregulated) were identified with a 2-fold m6A change (Figure 8—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by MeRIP-seq data presented in Figure 8—figure supplement 1E.

claim: RNA-seq analysis identified 3,213 upregulated and 809 downregulated genes at 5 dpr compared with sham group.
source: RNA-seq analysis identified 3,213 upregulated and 809 downregulated genes at 5 dpr compared with sham group (Figure 8—figure supplement 3A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data presented in Figure 8—figure supplement 3A, B.

claim: Gene-set enrichment analysis (GSEA) revealed that cardiac muscle cell development and proliferation gene sets are related to neonatal heart injury and regeneration.
source: Gene-set enrichment analysis (GSEA) revealed that cardiac muscle cell development and proliferation gene sets are related to neonatal heart injury and regeneration (Figure 8—figure supplement 3C, D).
evidence: This claim is supported by GSEA analysis of RNA-seq data presented in Figure 8—figure supplement 3C, D.

claim: 333 overlapped genes between the m6A-tagged and mRNA-upregulated genes were identified at 5 dpr.
source: Based on RNA-seq and m6A-seq data, 333 overlapped genes between the m6A-tagged and mRNA-upregulated genes were identified at 5 dpr (Figure 8—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by conjoint analysis of RNA-seq and MeRIP-seq data presented in Figure 8—figure supplement 4A.

claim: The silencing of Fgf16, rather than Mis12 and Six5, significantly induced G1-phase cell cycle arrest in H9c2 cells.
source: We found that the silencing of Fgf16, rather than Mis12 and Six5, significantly induced G1-phase cell cycle arrest (Figure 8—figure supplement 4G-J).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data presented in Figure 8—figure supplement 4G-J.

claim: Fgf16 silencing suppressed the proliferation of primary cardiomyocytes isolated from neonatal mice, as demonstrated by double staining with Ki67 and cTnT.
source: Importantly, Fgf16 silencing also suppressed the proliferation of primary cardiomyocytes isolated from neonatal mice, which was demonstrated by double staining with Ki67 and cTnT (Figure 8A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence staining data presented in Figure 8A and B.

claim: The decreased proliferation of primary cardiomyocytes induced by Fgf16 silencing was confirmed by nuclear EdU incorporation.
source: Moreover, the decreased proliferation of primary cardiomyocytes induced by Fgf16 silencing was further confirmed by nuclear EdU incorporation (Figure 8C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by EdU incorporation assay data presented in Figure 8C and D.

claim: GSEA analysis indicated the involvement of Fgf pathway in neonatal heart regeneration.
source: GSEA revealed that the Fgf signaling pathway is related to neonatal heart regeneration (Figure 8E).
evidence: This claim is supported by GSEA analysis presented in Figure 8E.

claim: MeRIP-seq showed a great increase (about 10 folds) in the m6A peaks of Fgf16 mRNA during neonatal heart injury.
source: Importantly, MeRIP-seq showed a great increase (about 10 folds) in the m6A peaks of Fgf16 mRNA during neonatal heart injury (Figure 8F, upper panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by MeRIP-seq data presented in Figure 8F.

claim: The RNA-seq reads were only increased by 2 folds in the Fgf16 mRNA during neonatal heart injury.
source: However, the RNA-seq reads were only increased by 2 folds in the Fgf16 mRNA (Figure 8F, lower panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data presented in Figure 8F.

claim: m6A enrichment in Fgf16 was remarkably upregulated by Mettl3 overexpression in the regenerating heart at 5 dpr.
source: To further determine whether and how m6A modification regulates Fgf16 mRNA levels, we performed m6A-RIP-qPCR and found that m6A enrichment in Fgf16 was remarkably upregulated by Mettl3 overexpression (Figure 8G) but suppressed by Mettl3 silencing (Figure 8H) in the regenerating heart at 5 dpr.
evidence: This claim is supported by m6A-RIP-qPCR data presented in Figure 8G.

claim: m6A enrichment in Fgf16 was suppressed by Mettl3 silencing in the regenerating heart at 5 dpr.
source: To further determine whether and how m6A modification regulates Fgf16 mRNA levels, we performed m6A-RIP-qPCR and found that m6A enrichment in Fgf16 was remarkably upregulated by Mettl3 overexpression (Figure 8G) but suppressed by Mettl3 silencing (Figure 8H) in the regenerating heart at 5 dpr.
evidence: This claim is supported by m6A-RIP-qPCR data presented in Figure 8H.

claim: Fgf16 mRNA expression at 5 dpr was significantly suppressed by Mettl3 overexpression.
source: However, Fgf16 mRNA expression at 5 dpr was significantly suppressed by Mettl3 overexpression (Figure 8I).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data presented in Figure 8I.

claim: Mettl3 silencing significantly increased the mRNA levels of Fgf16 at 5 dpr.
source: As expected, Mettl3 silencing significantly increased the mRNA levels of Fgf16 (Figure 8I).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data presented in Figure 8I.

claim: Mettl3 knockdown significantly increased the production of Fgf16 protein in the regenerating heart at 5 dpr.
source: Our data showed that Mettl3 knockdown (Figure 8J) significantly increased the production of Fgf16 protein in the regenerating heart at 5 dpr (Figure 8K).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data presented in Figure 8J and K.

claim: Mettl3 knockdown increased the protein levels of Fgf16 at p8 (equal to 5 dpr in the injured heart) in the uninjured neonatal heart, although the expression levels were lower than that in the injured heart at 5 dpr.
source: Mettl3 knockdown also increased the protein levels of Fgf16 at p8 (equal to 5 dpr in the injured heart) in the uninjured neonatal heart, although the expression levels were lower than that in the injured heart at 5 dpr (Figure 8L).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data presented in Figure 8L.

claim: Fgf16 expressions in CMs were greatly increased by Mettl3 deficiency compared with control hearts during regeneration.
source: As shown in Figure 8M, Fgf16 expressions in CMs were greatly increased by Mettl3 deficiency compared with control hearts during regeneration.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data presented in Figure 8M.

claim: The expression of Fgf16 in nCMs was decreased in the Mettl3-deficient hearts compared with controls during regeneration.
source: However, the expression of Fgf16 in nCMs was decreased in the Mettl3-deficient hearts compared with controls.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data presented in Figure 8M.

claim: Fgf16 expression level in CMs is significantly higher than that in nCMs during heart regeneration regardless of Mettl3 deficiency or not.
source: Importantly, Fgf16 expression level in CMs is significantly higher than that in nCMs during heart regeneration regardless of Mettl3 deficiency or not (Figure 8M).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data presented in Figure 8M.

claim: Both the luciferase activity and mRNA levels of wild-type Fgf16-fused reporter gene were greatly suppressed by Mettl3 overexpression.
source: For the wild-type reporter gene, both the luciferase activity and mRNA levels were greatly suppressed by Mettl3 overexpression, and this suppression was significantly blocked by Mettl3 catalytic mutant (ΔMettl3) and the mutation of m6A consensus sequence in Fgf16 (ΔFgf16), respectively (Figure 8—figure supplement 5B, C).
evidence: This claim is supported by luciferase reporter assay data presented in Figure 8—figure supplement 5B, C.

claim: The suppression of wild-type Fgf16-fused reporter gene by Mettl3 overexpression was significantly blocked by Mettl3 catalytic mutant (ΔMettl3) and the mutation of m6A consensus sequence in Fgf16 (ΔFgf16).
source: For the wild-type reporter gene, both the luciferase activity and mRNA levels were greatly suppressed by Mettl3 overexpression, and this suppression was significantly blocked by Mettl3 catalytic mutant (ΔMettl3) and the mutation of m6A consensus sequence in Fgf16 (ΔFgf16), respectively (Figure 8—figure supplement 5B, C).
evidence: This claim is supported by luciferase reporter assay data presented in Figure 8—figure supplement 5B, C.

claim: siMettl3-increased CM proliferation was significantly blocked by siFgf16 treatment in primary cardiomyocytes.
source: Ki67 and cTnT double staining revealed that siMettl3 treatment greatly increased the percentage of Ki67+ cTnT+ cells compared with control group, indicating an increased proliferation level of CMs. However, siMettl3-increased CM proliferation was significantly blocked by siFgf16 treatment (Figure 8—figure supplement 6A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence staining data presented in Figure 8—figure supplement 6A, B.

claim: shMettl3 injection increased CM proliferation in ventricular apex at 5 dpr compared with control groups, but this was significantly blocked by shFgf16 injection.
source: In agreement with in vitro data, immunofluorescent staining revealed that shMettl3 injection increased CM proliferation in ventricular apex at 5 dpr compared with control groups. However, the shMettl3-increased CM proliferation was significantly blocked by shFgf16 injection (Figure 8—figure supplement 6D, E).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence staining data presented in Figure 8—figure supplement 6D, E.

claim: Scar size in the cardiac apex at 14 dpr was greatly decreased by Mettl3 deficiency compared with control groups, but this was significantly blocked by Fgf16 knockdown.
source: In addition, histological analysis revealed that scar size in the cardiac apex at 14 dpr was greatly decreased by Mettl3 deficiency compared with control groups. However, this shMettl3-induced decrease in scar size was significantly blocked by Fgf16 knockdown (Figure 8—figure supplement 6F, G).
evidence: This claim is supported by Masson's trichrome staining data presented in Figure 8—figure supplement 6F, G.

claim: shMettl3-increased left ventricular systolic function was significantly blocked by shFgf16.
source: In consistent, cardiac function analysis revealed that shMettl3-inceased left ventricular systolic function was significantly blocked by shFgf16 (Figure 8—figure supplement 6H-J).
evidence: This claim is supported by echocardiography data presented in Figure 8—figure supplement 6H-J.

claim: Mettl14 and Fto knockdown did not significantly change the expression level of Fgf16 in primary cardiomyocytes.
source: Our data showed that Mettl14 and Fto knockdown (Figure 8—figure supplement 7A, B) did not significantly change the expression level of Fgf16 in primary cardiomyocytes (Figure 8—figure supplement 7C).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data presented in Figure 8—figure supplement 7A-C.

claim: The percentage of Ki67-positive cardiomyocytes in siMettl14- and siFto-treated groups was comparable with control group.
source: Moreover, the percentage of Ki67-positive cardiomyocytes in siMettl14- and siFto-treated groups was comparable with control group (Figure 8—figure supplement 7D, E).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence staining data presented in Figure 8—figure supplement 7D, E.

claim: Silencing of Ythdf2 rather than Ythdf1 elevated the expression of Fgf16 up to 6-fold in primary cardiomyocytes.
source: Silencing of Ythdf2 rather than Ythdf1 elevated the expression of Fgf16 up to 6-fold in primary cardiomyocytes (Figure 8—figure supplement 8A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data presented in Figure 8—figure supplement 8A and B.

claim: Relative Fgf16 mRNA level was increased in Ythdf2-deficient cardiomyocytes in comparison to control cells after Actinomycin-D treatment for 3–6 hr.
source: Moreover, we performed RNA decay assay and found that relative Fgf16 mRNA level was increased in Ythdf2-deficient cardiomyocytes in comparison to control cells after Actinomycin-D treatment for 3–6 hr (Figure 8—figure supplement 8C), indicating the decreased degradation of Fgf16 mRNA.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA decay assay data presented in Figure 8—figure supplement 8C.

claim: Ythdf2 remarkably enriched in Fgf16 mRNA in normal primary cardiomyocytes, whereas this relative enrichment was significantly suppressed in Mettl3-deficient cardiomyocytes.
source: Our data showed that Ythdf2 remarkably enriched in Fgf16 mRNA in normal primary cardiomyocytes, whereas this relative enrichment was significantly suppressed in Mettl3-deficient cardiomyocytes (Figure 8—figure supplement 8D).
evidence: This claim is supported by RIP-qPCR data presented in Figure 8—figure supplement 8D.

claim: The relative luciferase activity of wild-type Fgf16 reporter gene was greatly increased by Ythdf2 knockdown.
source: Our data showed that the relative luciferase activity of wild-type reporter gene was greatly increased by Ythdf2 knockdown.
evidence: This claim is supported by luciferase reporter assay data presented in Figure 8—figure supplement 8F.

claim: For mutant Fgf16 reporter plasmid, Ythdf2 knockdown did not alter the relative luciferase activity.
source: For mutant Fgf16 reporter plasmid, Ythdf2 knockdown did not alter the relative luciferase activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by luciferase reporter assay data presented in Figure 8—figure supplement 8F.

claim: The mutant Fgf16 reporter plasmid showed increased luciferase activity in normal cells (siNC) compared with the wild-type reporter plasmid.
source: However, the mutant Fgf16 reporter plasmid showed increased luciferase activity in normal cells (siNC) compared with the wild-type reporter plasmid (Figure 8—figure supplement 8F).
evidence: This claim is supported by luciferase reporter assay data presented in Figure 8—figure supplement 8F.

claim: The protein level of Fgf16 in neonatal heart was slightly elevated by AAV9-Fgf16 virus.
source: Our data showed that the protein level of Fgf16 in neonatal heart was slightly elevated by AAV9-Fgf16 virus.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data presented in Figure 9C.

claim: AAV9-ΔFgf16 remarkably increased the expression of Fgf16 protein compared with AAV9-Fgf16 group.
source: However, AAV9-ΔFgf16 remarkably increased the expression of Fgf16 protein compared with AAV9-Fgf16 group (Figure 9C).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data presented in Figure 9C.

claim: There was no significant difference in the proliferation of cardiomyocytes in cardiac apex in AAV9-Fgf16 group in comparison to AAV9-NC group at 5 dpr.
source: Ki67 staining showed that there was no significant difference in the proliferation of cardiomyocytes in cardiac apex in AAV9-Fgf16 group in comparison to AAV9-NC group.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence staining data presented in Figure 9D and E.

claim: AAV9-ΔFgf16 significantly increased the percentage of Ki67+ cTnT+ cells compared with AAV9-Fgf16 group at 5 dpr.
source: However, AAV9-ΔFgf16 significantly increased the percentage of Ki67+ cTnT+ cells compared with AAV9-Fgf16 group (Figure 9D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence staining data presented in Figure 9D and E.

claim: The percentage of pH3+ cTnT+ cells was significantly elevated by AAV9-ΔFgf16 compared with AAV9-Fgf16 at 5 dpr, although AAV9-Fgf16 only slightly promoted the percentage of pH3+ cTnT+ cells in comparison to AAV9-NC.
source: The percentage of pH3+ cTnT+ cells was also significantly elevated by AAV9-ΔFgf16 compared with AAV9-Fgf16, although AAV9-Fgf16 only slightly promoted the percentage of pH3+ cTnT+ cells in comparison to AAV9-NC (Figure 9F and G).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence staining data presented in Figure 9F and G.

claim: Increased percentage of AurkB+ cardiomyocytes was detected in cardiac apex in AAV9-ΔFgf16 group compared with AAV9-Fgf16 group at 5 dpr.
source: Moreover, increased percentage of AurkB+ cardiomyocytes was also detected in cardiac apex in AAV9-ΔFgf16 group compared with AAV9-Fgf16 group (Figure 9H1).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence staining data presented in Figure 9H and I.

claim: Trichrome staining results revealed a decreased fibrotic scar size at 14 dpr in AAV9-ΔFgf16 group compared with AAV9-Fgf16 group.
source: As expected, trichrome staining results further revealed a decreased fibrotic scar size at 14 dpr in AAV9-ΔFgf16 group compared with AAV9-Fgf16 group (Figure 9J), indicating the accelerated heart regeneration.
evidence: This claim is supported by Masson's trichrome staining data presented in Figure 9J.

claim: There was a higher left ventricular systolic function in AAV9-ΔFgf16 group compared with AAV9-Fgf16 group at 14 dpr.
source: Consistent with these results, cardiac function analysis revealed that there was a higher left ventricular systolic function in AAV9-ΔFgf16 group compared with AAV9-Fgf16 group (Figure 9K–M).
evidence: This claim is supported by echocardiography data presented in Figure 9K-M.

claim: Mettl3 post-transcriptionally reduces Fgf16 mRNA levels through an m6A-Ythdf2-dependent pathway, thereby controlling cardiomyocyte proliferation and heart regeneration.
source: Our data demonstrate that Mettl3 post-transcriptionally reduces Fgf16 mRNA levels through an m6A-Ythdf2-dependen pathway, thereby controlling cardiomyocyte proliferation and heart regeneration.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence including MeRIP-seq, RNA-seq, RIP-qPCR, luciferase reporter assays, and functional studies presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Mettl3 is a key myocardial methylase that regulates cardiac m6A.
source: We identified Mettl3 as a key myocardial methylase that regulates cardiac m6A and provided a novel characterization of Mettl3-mediated m6A modification during heart regeneration in mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that Mettl3 expression and m6A levels are correlated during heart regeneration.

claim: Targeting the Mettl3-mediated m6A modification of Fgf16 may represent a promising therapeutic strategy for promoting the proliferation of cardiomyocytes in mammals.
source: Targeting the Mettl3-mediated m6A modification of Fgf16 may represent a promising therapeutic strategy for promoting the proliferation of cardiomyocytes in mammals.
evidence: This claim is based on speculation about potential therapeutic applications of the findings.
